pronunciation.approximation: 'HWAH-noong' — the second syllable ends in a velar nasal, like the 'ng' in 'song'. The capitalised form marks the heavenly prince as a proper noun.

kin.form: 桓雄 (hwan 'majestic, spreading' + ung 'hero, male') — the Sino-Korean character form.

kin.label: Relatives
kin.form: Hwanin 桓因 ('Lord of Heaven'), his father, and Dangun 檀君, his son — all three named in the Samguk Yusa.

pronunciation.note: Hwanung is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the romanised form preserves no diacritic or distinctive letter that the ASCII form loses. Only the capital distinguishes the restored name — the capital that marks a heavenly prince from a common string.

domains.title: Hwanung, the Heavenly Prince
domains.subtitle: descended bringer of law, grain, and civilisation
domains.lead: Hwanung is the heavenly prince who descends from Hwanin's court to bring law, grain, and the arts of civilisation to earth. In the Samguk Yusa he carries three heavenly seals, founds a sacred city beneath a sandalwood tree, and fathers Dangun, first king of the Korean people.

cards.name: Son of Hwanin
cards.desc: Hwanung carries the authority of heaven as the delegate of his father, the Lord of Heaven.

cards.name: Descended to Taebaek
cards.desc: He descends beneath a sandalwood tree on a high mountain, the sacred entry point between heaven and earth.

cards.name: Law and Agriculture
cards.desc: He teaches the people law, grain, medicine, and the crafts that define civilised life.

cards.name: Father of Dangun
cards.desc: His union with Ungnyeo produces Dangun, the first ancestor and king of the Korean people.

symbols.name: Sandalwood tree

symbols.meaning: Tokens of delegated sovereignty that authorise Hwanung to rule the human realm.

symbols.name: Wind, rain, clouds, grain
symbols.meaning: The cosmic departments over which Hwanung presides as culture-bringer.

symbols.name: Clouds and mist
symbols.meaning: The celestial medium through which the heavenly prince travels between realms.

mythology.lead: Hwanung's cycle, preserved in the Samguk Yusa, is the founding charter of Korean civilisation: a heavenly prince descends with seals of delegated authority, teaches law, medicine, and agriculture, and fathers Dangun, first king of the Korean people. The myth binds kingship to cosmic order and anchors the nation to a sacred mountain.

myths.title: Three Thousand Follow One Prince
myths.text: In the Samguk Yusa (Wanggok, 'Ancient Kingdoms' chapter), Hwanung, son of Hwanin — the Lord of Heaven — looks down upon the world of human beings and longs to govern it. He asks his father's leave; Hwanin grants him three heavenly seals and three thousand retainers, and the prince descends. His landing place is a sandalwood tree on the summit of Taebaek-san, where he founds the City of the Gods (Sin-si) and rules the affairs of humankind: wind, rain, cloud, and grain. The descent is not exile but delegation: Hwanung carries his father's mandate, and the seals he bears are the charter of his rule. The myth establishes the Korean pattern of legitimate sovereignty — authority descends from heaven only when a worthy agent asks for it, and it binds the ruler to care for harvests, health, and law rather than to mere dominion.

myths.title: Wind, Rain, Cloud, and Grain
myths.text: Hwanung's government is a civilisation kit. The Samguk Yusa credits him with teaching the people the fundamental arts: agriculture and the calendar, the loom and the making of clothing, the curing of disease, and the rules by which society lives. When drought strikes, he prays at the altar and the rains come. His company of three hundred and sixty officers mirrors the round of the year — a bureaucracy as cosmic as it is political. The same chapter-cycle remembers him as judge of the boundary between human custom and animal nature: in the tale of the woodcutter who married a tigress, whose son's filial trials reach Hwanung's tribunal, the prince weighs a son's duty against a mother's beasthood and finds for the human claim. The myth's claim is total: nothing in Korean life — food, cloth, health, justice — stands outside the mandate the prince brought down from heaven.

myths.title: Garlic and Mugwort for a Hundred Days
myths.text: A bear and a tiger, sharing a cave, pray to Hwanung to become human. The prince gives them twenty cloves of garlic and a bundle of mugwort, commanding them to eat of these and stay out of the sunlight for one hundred days. The tiger cannot endure the dark and abandons the test; the bear obeys, and on the twenty-first day her dark hair falls away and she stands a woman — Ungnyeo, 'the bear-woman'. She has no husband, and prays beneath the sandalwood tree for a child; Hwanung hears her prayer, joins with her, and she bears a son, Dangun. Only one account preserves this narrative in full — the Samguk Yusa of 1281, itself compiling much older material — but its symbolism is transparent: endurance and obedience to the prescribed rite transform the beast, impatience forfeits the prize. The bear who becomes the mother of the nation is Korean myth's charter for the virtue of perseverance.

myths.title: Dangun and the Mountain
myths.text: Dangun grows to found Gojoseon — 'Old Joseon' — and the chronicle tradition, carried by the Samguk Yusa from the Tongguk t'onggam, dates his accession to the year corresponding to 2333 BCE, still celebrated as the founding of the Korean nation. He rules, the sources say, for some fifteen hundred years, until the age of Jizi (Kija), the righteous minister of the Chinese Shang, brings a rival civilisation to the peninsula; then Dangun withdraws from rule and becomes a mountain god (sansin), the guardian numen of the heights. The withdrawal completes the cycle his father began: heaven descended in Hwanung, walked the earth in Dangun, and returned to the mountains as the protective spirit of the land itself. The myth performs the classic work of foundation charters — it converts geography into genealogy, making the Korean landscape the body of a single divine family.

etymology.derivation: The name combines 桓 (hwan, 'majestic, spreading') and 雄 (ung, 'male, hero'). Read 환웅 in Korean, it denotes the heroic son of heaven whose descent initiates Korean civilisation.

lore.originalScriptNote: Korean names may be written in Hangul, the indigenous Korean alphabet, and sometimes in Hanja, the Sino-Korean character set. For Hwanung, the Hangul form is 환웅 and the Hanja form is 桓雄 — the forms preserved in the Samguk Yusa. The ASCII form hwanung is a technological compromise; the capitalised restoration Hwanung is the scholarly citation form.
lore.syncretism: Confucian readers of the Joseon era found in Hwanung a model of hyo — the son who serves his father's will by governing well — and the Samguk Yusa itself, written by the monk Iryeon, frames the descent through Buddhist eyes as a bodhisattva-like mission of compassion toward suffering beings. Daoist parallels came easily: an immortal descending to a sacred mountain and founding a city of gods reads like the Korean cousin of the Queen Mother of the West's mountain courts. Under the twentieth century the story was nationalised: the religion of Daejonggyo, founded in 1909, worships Hwanin, Hwanung, and Dangun as a trinity, and Korean nationalists dated events by the Dangun calendar; in North Korea the reconstructed tomb of Dangun at Kangdong (1994) claims the lineage for the state. What began as a monk's charter became a modern identity.
lore.culturalLegacy: Hwanung's legacy is celebrated every 3 October, Gaecheonjeol — 'Festival of the Opening of Heaven' — when the descent is reenacted at the Chamseongdan altars, most famously on Taebaeksan, the traditional landing site, and at the Manisan Chamseongdan on Ganghwa Island, where Joseon kings once offered prayer. The myth anchors Korean educational culture: foundation pageants, museum dioramas, and school curricula from Seoul to Pyongyang stage the bear's transformation and the descent beneath the sandalwood. The name lives on in institutions — universities, mountain lodges, cultural foundations — and in the phrase 'Dangun minjok', the Dangun nation, still current in identity discourse. Few foundation myths anywhere remain so busy: thirteen centuries after Iryeon wrote it down, the story of the prince who asked to come down still organises how Koreans imagine where they come from.
lore.extendedMeditation: Hwanung is the ruler who asked permission to rule. Other founding myths in the neighbourhood begin with conquest, theft, or disaster; the Korean charter begins with a request. The prince sees the suffering world below, petitions his father, and descends not as master but as delegate — carrying seals, not a sword. His myth quietly proposes a theory of government: authority is legitimate only when it is asked for on behalf of others, and it is proven only by service — rain prayed down in drought, medicine taught, law spoken. Even his marriage to the bear-woman follows the same grammar: he answers a prayer. The myth thus remembers civilisation itself as a response to need. In an age that too often treats power as a prize, the heavenly prince who knelt to be sent is a quietly radical ancestor.

lore.archaeology: No artefact names Hwanung: the myth's only early witness is textual, in Iryeon's Samguk Yusa of 1281, which preserves older oral and ritual material. The material anchor is the ritual landscape. The Chamseongdan — 'altar of the heavenly deity' — on Taebaeksan, rebuilt in stone in later centuries, marks the traditional descent site, and the great Chamseongdan on Manisan, Ganghwa Island, where Joseon kings performed the state sacrifices, stands in the same cultic geography. In 1993–94 North Korea reconstructed the supposed mausoleum of Dangun at Kangdong near Pyongyang as a monumental shrine. Modern reenactments at Taebaeksan each Gaecheonjeol give the myth a living present: the mountain itself, not any object, is the evidence Koreans point to.
